Generates Hyperlambda endpoints wrapping the operations you select from an OpenAPI specification.

The specification is re-parsed here rather than trusted from the caller, and only the operations
named in [operations] are generated. Each generated endpoint invokes the upstream API server-side,
reading its credential from configuration at invocation time - so the credential is never written
into the generated file, and never reaches whoever invokes the endpoint.

Generated endpoints are ordinary endpoints, which means they immediately become MCP tools and can
be added as AI functions, gated by the roles given in [auth].

Parses an OpenAPI specification and returns what can be imported from it.

Supply the specification either as a [url] we fetch, or inline as [spec]. Returns the servers
declared by the specification, its security schemes, and one entry per operation - which is what
the caller picks from before importing.

Handles OpenAPI 3 and Swagger 2.0, in JSON or YAML, since both versions and both formats are
common in the wild. Their differences are resolved here, so everything downstream sees one shape.

Exchanges an OpenID Connect authorization code for an application JWT token

Verifies the specified OpenID Connect JWT Token and returns a valid application JWT token accordingly.

This will verify the token towards the issuers of all OpenID providers registered in the system,
refusing to fetch meta data from issuers we do not recognise, download any public keys to verify
the signature, and return the email, name and issuer from the token.

If it succeeds it will return a new application specific JWT token.
If it fails it will throw an exception.

Notice, the endpoint will only return valid JWT tokens for OIDC providers that are
registered in the system with existing configurations. See the "openid-providers.get.hl" file for
details about how to register a new OIDC provider in the app.

Returns all supported OpenID Connect providers the system supports, if any.

Notice, this endpoint can be extended by creating a slot named [magic.openid.providers-XYZ]
that returns additional OpenID providers, which will inject new providers into the core of the system.

See the code for the slot named [magic.openid.providers.google] for an example.

Emails a magnetic link to the specified user, letting them sign in without
their password and change it once they arrive.

The [user] argument is either a username or an email address. When it is a
username the email is taken from the user's "email" extra field, so a user
without an email on file behaves exactly like a user that does not exist.

Notice, this endpoint deliberately returns the same result whether or not
the user exists, whether or not they have an email address, and whether or
not SMTP is configured. Anything else turns a public endpoint into an
oracle for discovering which usernames and email addresses are real.

This file will setup your system, changing its default JWT secret, create the magic database,
and insert a root user - Unless the database, and/or root user exists from before.

Notice, if the root user exists from before, this file will change its password.
However, you cannot setup the system twice, unless you manually change the JWT secret to a value
that's less than 50 characters in length.

Since the setup process always create a JWT secret that's longer than 50 character, this allows you
to "reset" your root password by removing the JWT secret, at which point you can login with
root/root again to your backend.
Returns the setup status of the system
